title: Minnesota tried to stop AI from undressing women. A court has put the law on hold.
subtitle: An appeals court has temporarily blocked the first US state law aimed at companies that supply one-click “nudification” tools. The order is not a finding that synthetic sexual abuse is protected speech—but Minnesota’s failure to make lack of consent an explicit element of the law has given xAI a serious constitutional argument.
author: ATHENA
body:
Archive report — originally reported 3 October 2026. The reporting below reflects that date.

A US appeals court has paused Minnesota’s new restriction on artificial-intelligence tools that can turn an ordinary photograph into a realistic sexual image, giving Elon Musk’s xAI temporary relief while its constitutional challenge proceeds.

The Eighth US Circuit Court of Appeals granted an injunction on 2 October, according to Reuters. The order prevents Minnesota from enforcing the law against xAI during the appeal. It does not strike down the statute, decide that the company will ultimately win or declare that creating non-consensual intimate imagery is protected conduct. The case remains open. Reuters.

https://www.reuters.com/world/us-appeals-court-blocks-minnesotas-ai-nudification-law-now-xai-lawsuit-2026-10-02/

The distinction matters because the dispute is not about whether fabricated sexual images can cause real harm. Minnesota lawmakers heard directly from women whose photographs had been turned into pornography. xAI says it also opposes non-consensual sexual imagery and has safeguards intended to stop it.

The legal question is narrower and more difficult: can a state hold the maker of a general-purpose AI product responsible for giving users a simple route to create these images, and did Minnesota define the prohibited output precisely enough to survive the US Constitution’s protection of speech?

## The law targets the tool—not only the person who misuses it

Minnesota’s law took effect on 1 August. It prohibits the owner or controller of a website, application, software program or other electronic service from allowing people to access, download or use a service to “nudify” an image. It also bars advertising or promoting such a service.

The statute defines nudification as altering or generating an image or video so that it appears to show an intimate part that was not visible in the original. The output must be realistic enough that a reasonable person would believe the depicted body part belongs to an identifiable individual. A service requiring “substantial” individual technical or artistic skill is exempt, meaning the law is principally directed at automated, readily accessible tools rather than professional image-editing software. Minnesota Session Laws, Chapter 72.

https://www.revisor.mn.gov/laws/2026/0/Session+Law/Chapter/72/

That product-level approach is significant. Laws against harassment, sexual exploitation or distribution of intimate images generally focus on what a perpetrator does with an image. Minnesota also asks whether a company designed or supplied the mechanism that made the abuse quick, scalable and available to people without specialist skills.

The consequences are substantial. A person depicted in an unlawful image may seek compensation, punitive damages, an injunction and legal fees. The attorney general may seek a civil penalty of up to $500,000 for each unlawful access, download or use. Money collected from those penalties is assigned to services for survivors of sexual assault, domestic violence, child abuse and other crimes.

Those remedies recognise that a fake image can produce real costs: time away from work or school, demands for removal, legal fees, fear that the image will reach relatives or employers and the loss of control over one’s public identity.

## Women’s testimony moved the issue from theory to law

The measure passed with overwhelming bipartisan support after lawmakers heard from three Minnesota women targeted by a man who used photographs taken from private Facebook accounts to make fabricated pornography. Legislative reporting said the perpetrator had produced images of more than 80 women.

During the April House debate, bill author Representative Jessica Hanson described consequences extending beyond embarrassment: disrupted work, fear for personal safety, concern for children and reluctance to leave home. The women’s testimony helped make clear that “nothing physically happened” is not an adequate description of the violation. A recognisable face, a plausible body and digital distribution can make the false event socially consequential even though it never occurred. Minnesota House Session Daily.

https://www.house.mn.gov/SessionDaily/Story/19118

But recognising the harm does not resolve every drafting question. The same House debate included an objection from Representative Drew Roach, the sole vote against the bill, who argued that lawmakers should focus on perpetrators. The final law instead reaches both misuse and the design or availability of a tool.

That is precisely what makes it potentially powerful—and constitutionally vulnerable.

## xAI’s strongest objection is one word the statute does not contain: consent

xAI argues that the law regulates expressive content and is therefore subject to demanding First Amendment review. Its challenge says Minnesota’s definition does not require prosecutors or plaintiffs to prove that the depicted person did not consent, that the creator knew consent was absent or that the image was distributed.

The company also argues that “intimate part” is broad enough to cover images involving a breast, buttocks or inner thigh, including material that could be artistic, satirical or consensual. In xAI’s account, the law therefore captures more than the non-consensual sexual abuse that lawmakers repeatedly described. These are the company’s legal claims, not findings the appellate court has adopted. xAI’s motion for an injunction.

https://reason.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/101111696305.pdf

That omission is not merely a technical lawyer’s complaint. If the state’s objective is to stop non-consensual sexual imagery, making absence of consent an explicit element could bring the statutory language closer to the harm it seeks to prevent. The state may respond that consent is difficult for a platform to verify and that a service built to generate realistic nudity from an identifiable person’s photograph creates a foreseeable risk regardless of what an individual user declares.

The case will force courts to consider both problems: a law cannot be broader than the Constitution allows, but a consent rule that exists only on paper may be ineffective when the product never checks whether the depicted person agreed.

## The court has not yet answered the constitutional question

US District Judge Donovan Frank denied xAI’s initial request to suspend the law on 4 September. His ruling rested principally on the company’s delay in seeking emergency relief and its failure to demonstrate irreparable harm—not on a final conclusion that the statute was constitutional.

Frank described the First Amendment questions as complex and said they required fuller consideration. He nevertheless found, at that preliminary stage, that the balance of harms and the public interest favoured the state. District court order.

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/minnesota/mndce/0:2026cv03425/235231/54/

xAI appealed on 9 September. The Eighth Circuit’s decision to issue an injunction while that appeal is heard changes what Minnesota may enforce for now, but the court has not yet published a final merits decision in the appeal. Minnesota’s attorney general’s office told Reuters it was disappointed and would continue defending the law.

That procedural history should temper claims from either side. Supporters cannot say a court has upheld the statute’s substance; opponents cannot say it has been invalidated. What exists is a temporary pause imposed by a higher court while it examines the dispute.

## Company safeguards are part of the evidence—not a substitute for law

xAI says its Grok Imagine product has “rigorous protections” and that it is pursuing users who evade its blockers. In court filings, the company has pointed to its rules against non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual-abuse material.

Those policies matter, but their existence does not establish that they work consistently. In January, a Reuters test involving nine reporters found that Grok produced sexualised edits in 45 of 55 prompts in one round and 29 of 43 in a second. The system did not create full nudity or explicit sex acts in that test, and the exercise was a limited newsroom spot check rather than a representative or independently reproducible audit of every user, model version or safeguard. It cannot establish Grok’s current failure rate. It did show that announced restrictions could be circumvented under the conditions tested. Reuters investigation.

https://www.reuters.com/business/despite-new-curbs-elon-musks-grok-times-produces-sexualized-images-even-when-2026-02-03/

This is the larger accountability gap. A company may update its model or moderation system overnight; a survivor usually cannot inspect the product’s internal rules, training data or enforcement logs. Voluntary safeguards can improve faster than legislation, but they can also be relaxed, inconsistently applied or difficult to verify.

Minnesota’s law tries to place part of that burden on the supplier. xAI’s lawsuit asks whether the state has done so through a rule that is too broad.

## A stronger law would protect consent without abandoning product responsibility

The injunction should not reduce this debate to a choice between unrestricted AI and a ban on difficult or provocative images. A more durable framework can distinguish consensual adult expression from the automated sexual violation of an identifiable person.

That would mean defining non-consent clearly; setting a meaningful knowledge or reckless-disregard standard for companies; requiring accessible reporting, rapid review and evidence preservation; and imposing stronger safeguards when a depicted person may be a child. It would also mean auditing whether age gates, prompt filters, account sanctions and removal systems function in practice rather than accepting policy pages as proof.

Care is needed not to transfer the whole enforcement burden back to the women and girls depicted. A victim should not have to monitor every platform, repeatedly prove her identity or persuade each company that an image is false before a predictable product risk is taken seriously.

The law also needs room for legitimate visual expression, including satire, medical or educational material and consensual adult work. Protecting those uses does not require treating one-click sexualisation of a recognisable person as an unavoidable cost of innovation.

For now, Minnesota cannot rely on this statute against xAI while the appeal continues. Other laws, platform rules and possible civil claims have not disappeared, but they do not offer identical remedies and may not reach the product provider in the same way.

The appeal’s importance extends well beyond one company or one state. Generative AI has made the creation of plausible sexual images faster than the legal process for removing them. Courts and lawmakers now have to answer two questions at once: how to draft a rule narrow enough to respect lawful expression, and how to stop technological scale from turning women’s consent into an optional setting.

The Athena Perspective.
